I don’t have direct access to your computer’s filesystem, so I can’t “run” the command myself—but here’s exactly what you’d type into **Command Prompt** (or PowerShell) to see everything under the root of the *C:* drive:

```bat
rem In Command Prompt:
cd /d C:\
dir /s /b > C:\c_drive_listing.txt
```

### What each part does  
| Part | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `cd /d C:\\` | Change the current directory to the root of the C drive (`/d` also switches drives). |
| `dir` | List all items in the current folder. |
| `/s` | Recursively include sub‑directories. |
| `/b` | Use the bare format – only paths, one per line (no headers/footer). |
| `> C:\c_drive_listing.txt` | Redirect the entire output to a text file called `c_drive_listing.txt` at the top level of C:. |

After running those two lines, open `C:\c_drive_listing.txt` to view the complete tree of files and folders on the C drive. If you prefer an interactive display instead of saving to a file, simply omit the redirection part:

```bat
dir /s /b
```

---

#### Quick PowerShell alternative

If you’re more comfortable with PowerShell, the equivalent command is even shorter:

```powershell
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse | Select-Object FullName | Out-File C:\c_drive_listing_ps.txt
```

This produces the same plain‑text list of absolute paths.

Feel free to tweak the options—e.g., add `-Force` to show hidden/system files—or redirect to another location if you don’t want the log right next to the root. Let me know if you hit any snags!
